faq.q: How many living things are in soil?
faq.a: A teaspoon of healthy soil can contain 100 million to a billion bacteria, plus metres of fungal threads and thousands of tiny animals. A handful can hold more living things than there are people on Earth.

Springtails are tiny six-legged animals, often under 2 millimetres long, living in soil and leaf litter. A spring-like part under the body flicks them into the air to escape danger, and they feed on fungi and rotting plants.
asks: What are the tiny jumping bugs in soil?

faq.a: Nematodes are tiny roundworms, most too small to see. Soil is full of them: some eat bacteria or fungi, some hunt other tiny animals, and a few attack plant roots.
Soil life breaks down dead material, recycles nutrients, builds crumbly soil that holds air and water, and helps plants fight disease. Without it, soil would be lifeless dust.
asks: Why do plants need soil microbes?

faq.q: What makes soil smell earthy after rain?
faq.a: Much of that smell comes from geosmin, a substance made by soil bacteria called Streptomyces. Our noses can detect it in incredibly tiny amounts.

facts: The US Department of Agriculture estimates a teaspoon of healthy soil holds between 100 million and 1 billion bacteria.
The earthy smell of soil comes largely from geosmin, made by Streptomyces bacteria.
Mites are arachnids, relatives of spiders, and are among the most numerous animals in soil.
